sources.entry: Applying the Roofline Model - States the counter set and method that put a measured point on the plot in place of a hand-counted intensity.

summary.title: Applying the Roofline Model
summary.one_liner: Learn how to place measured (not hand-counted) kernels on a roofline plot by counting flops with Intel PMU events and memory traffic with uncore memory-controller counters.
keywords: peak performance and memory bandwidth bounds
takeaways: Work W is measured by summing floating point arithmetic/comparison counters, multiplying packed SSE double counts by 2 and AVX double counts by 4 (Sandy Bridge).
Memory traffic Q is better measured from raw memory-controller (uncore) read and write cache-line counters than from LLC miss counts, because of write-allocate, prefetching, and streaming effects.
Runtime T is taken from the time stamp counter; turbo boost and frequency scaling were disabled in BIOS for the experiments.
Cold cache runs are produced by changing the working data set each iteration (not flushing) and warm runs reuse data; the outer loop uses 20 repeats and reports the median with quartiles.
summary.summary: The paper explains how to produce roofline plots from measured data rather than back-of-the-envelope estimates, on recent Intel platforms. It defines operational intensity as flops divided by memory traffic, and measures work W with floating point counters, memory traffic Q with uncore memory-controller read/write cache-line counters (via an extended Intel PCM library), and runtime T with the time stamp counter. A nested-loop measurement strategy with median and quartile reporting is used, along with separate cold-cache and warm-cache procedures and a validation step on BLAS functions. The authors then apply these measurements to BLAS and FFT kernels across several Intel machines.
